description:
We are a team of industrial engineering students from El Salvador participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our background is in processes, risk analysis, indicators, and occupational health—skills we applied to a real space challenge: keeping astronauts healthy when communication with Earth is delayed and medical support is limited.

For this challenge we developed CrewVital, a web platform for space-crew health monitoring.
summary:
We developed CrewVital (Spanish/English) progressive web app for crew health monitoring on space missions. It turns NASA Human Research Program (HRP) hazards and vital-sign thresholds into a practical workflow for astronauts and the flight surgeon: record measurements, see traffic-light status (green/yellow/red), follow clear actions, and use emergency and mission-scenario guidance.

CrewVital addresses the challenge by connecting real NASA health and radiation reference knowledge to day-to-day decision support during ISS transit, lunar, Mars, or surface operations—without requiring login, so judges and crews can open it instantly. It also supports multi-crew tracking, optional real-time sync, and an onboard assistant (Kibo) that explains values using the app’s NASA-based knowledge.

It matters because deep-space crews face delayed communication and must act quickly when vitals leave safe ranges. CrewVital makes NASA science usable at the moment of care, improving situational awareness and coordination between crew and medical support.
details:
What it does and how it works:

CrewVital is a static PWA. Users choose a role (crew member or flight surgeon), select a mission environment, and log vital signs (blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, SpO2, glucose, sleep, mood, radiation dose, exercise, nutrition). Each value is classified against reference ranges linked to NASA HRP hazards and body regions. The dashboard shows what to do now; Diagnosis guides body-region or full checkups; Scenarios illustrate events such as solar storms; Emergency Mode walks through safety steps. Optional Firebase sync shares mission data across devices. Kibo, an onboard AI assistant, answers crew questions using only the app’s NASA-based knowledge base and the crew member’s latest measurements.

Benefits:

- No login: immediate access for crews and judges

- Clear escalation to the flight surgeon

- Works offline as a cached PWA after first visit (AI sync needs internet)

Intended impact:

Help crews detect early health deviations and act with NASA-aligned guidance when Earth support is delayed, improving safety and coordination with the flight surgeon.

Tools:

HTML, CSS, and JavaScript; Progressive Web App / service worker; GitHub Pages; Firebase Realtime Database (optional sync); Cloudflare Worker + Google Gemini (Kibo assistant); GitHub for version control; Cursor and Devin as coding assistants.

Creativity:

We combined industrial-engineering process thinking (roles, workflows, thresholds, escalation) with NASA HRP science in a mission-themed interface that is usable without technical training. Kibo presents AI support as a crew companion, with graceful messaging when communication energy is unavailable.

Factors considered:

Accessibility (simple language, bilingual, large emergency controls), low cost (free hosting and open web stack), energy/connectivity (core app works offline; AI is optional), and public access through 2027 judging.
